summary: Describes the tunnel broker model, which helps early IPv6 adopters connect to an existing IPv6 network such as the 6bone and obtain stable IPv6 addresses and DNS names. A broker sets up the tunnel on the user's behalf. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If your street has no road to a new town, a travel agent can arrange a bridge for you. A tunnel broker does that for early users of the new Internet address system.

subtitle: A service model for giving individual users and small sites access to IPv6

tldr.problem: Early adopters of IPv6 were isolated from the IPv6 Internet because they only had IPv4 connections. Setting up their own IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnels was too complex for individuals and small organizations.
tldr.mechanism: A Tunnel Broker is a service provider that automatically manages tunnel setup, assigns stable IPv6 addresses, registers DNS names, and operates tunnel servers on behalf of users who request a tunnel.
tldr.outcome: The Tunnel Broker model proved easier than manual configuration and more flexible than automatic tunneling. It enabled early IPv6 adoption by individuals while still allowing network providers to control and monitor tunnel usage.

facts.label: Core advantage
facts.value: Permanent IPv6 address with dynamic IPv4

today: RFC 3053 is an Informational RFC published in January 2001 that documents the Tunnel Broker framework for IPv6 transition. It has not been updated or obsoleted. The Tunnel Broker concept influenced later IPv6 transition mechanisms and demonstrated that centralized brokering could reduce configuration complexity for end users.

sections.title: The Tunnel Broker Model
sections.content:
The Tunnel Broker addresses a fundamental problem in IPv6 transition: early IPv6 adopters with only IPv4 Internet connectivity had no easy way to reach the growing IPv6 Internet. Manual tunnel configuration was complex and required extensive coordination. The Tunnel Broker model simplifies this by introducing a dedicated service provider (the broker) that acts as an intermediary.

The broker manages tunnels on behalf of users. A user supplies their IPv4 address and desired IPv6 prefix, and the broker sets up the tunnel end-point on a tunnel server, assigns stable IPv6 addresses, registers the addresses in DNS, and provides the user with all necessary configuration information. This approach serves early IPv6 adopters at a different segment of the market than the 6to4 mechanism, which focuses on isolated IPv6 sites connecting to each other rather than individuals joining the global IPv6 Internet.
sections.eli5: The Tunnel Broker is like a service that builds a bridge from your house to a new town for you. You tell it your address, and it constructs the bridge, makes sure mail gets addressed to you in the new town, and tells you everything you need to know to use it.

sections.title: Key Components
sections.content:
The Tunnel Broker model has three main functional elements. The Tunnel Broker (TB) is the user-facing component where clients register and request tunnels. It manages tunnel creation, modification, and deletion; chooses which tunnel server to use; allocates IPv6 prefixes; and registers addresses in DNS. The TB can be reached via the IPv4 Internet.

The Tunnel Server (TS) is a dual-stack router on the global Internet. When the TB sends a configuration order, the TS creates or modifies the server-side endpoint of the tunnel. It may also collect usage statistics for billing or management purposes. The DNS system registers and maintains the IPv6 addresses and names assigned to each tunnel endpoint, allowing clients to use domain names instead of remembering addresses.
sections.eli5: The broker takes your request, picks a tunnel server from its list, tells that server to create your tunnel, picks an address for you, and registers that address in the phone book. You then configure your side of the tunnel using the information the broker sent you.

sections.title: Using the Service
sections.content:
A client initiates the Tunnel Broker service by providing identity and credentials for authentication and access control. Once authorized, the client provides its IPv4 address, a DNS name for the tunnel endpoint, and whether it is a standalone host or a router needing multiple addresses.

The TB then designates a tunnel server, selects an IPv6 prefix (typically 48 bits for a site, 64 bits for a subnet, or 128 bits for a single host), sets a lifetime for the tunnel, and registers the IPv6 addresses in DNS. It then notifies the client with all tunnel parameters. The client configures its side of the tunnel, and the IPv6-over-IPv4 tunnel is ready for use, providing access to the 6bone or any other IPv6 network the tunnel server connects to.
sections.eli5: You ask the broker for a tunnel. It checks that you are who you say you are. You tell it your Internet address and what name you want. It picks a tunnel server, gives you a new address, writes it in the phone book, and tells you how to connect on your end.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Assignment and Management
sections.content:
The TB assigns global IPv6 addresses from its own address space to both the client side and server side of each tunnel. The lifetime of these addresses is designed to be relatively long and potentially longer than the client's IPv4 connection lifetime. This allows clients with dynamic IPv4 addresses (such as dial-up users getting different addresses via DHCP) to maintain stable, permanent IPv6 addresses and associated DNS names.

Tunnel management is critical because active tunnels consume resources on tunnel servers. Each tunnel is assigned a lifetime and removed after expiration unless the client requests an extension. For dial-up users, tunnel servers can report traffic statistics to the TB, allowing the broker to delete tunnels after a period of inactivity without waiting for the lifetime to expire. Alternatively, the TB can keep track of tunnel configuration even after the user disconnects, allowing rapid re-establishment using the same IPv6 addresses when the user reconnects with a different IPv4 address.
sections.eli5: You get a permanent address in the new system even though your Internet address keeps changing. The broker remembers your setup so if you reconnect later with a different Internet address, you can get the same new address back.

sections.title: Security and Known Limitations
sections.content:
The interactions between client, TB, TS, and DNS must all be secured. The client-TB interaction can use HTTPS and SSL to encrypt data and authenticate users via RADIUS or other AAA systems. TB-TS interaction can use secure SNMP. Dynamic DNS updates can use the DNS UPDATE protocol with security, or RSH commands over IPsec. If the TB provides configuration scripts to clients, these must be transferred over HTTPS to prevent malicious code execution.

A significant limitation of the Tunnel Broker model is that it does not work if the user is behind a NAT (Network Address Translation) box, because NAT prevents the tunnel server from reaching the user's IPv6 stack. Additionally, if a dial-up user disconnects without tearing down the tunnel, IPv6 traffic continues to be forwarded to the old IPv4 address, which may have been reassigned to another user, creating a confidentiality breach. This can be mitigated by implementing a keep-alive mechanism or aggressive timeout policies.
sections.eli5: Make sure the connection between you and the broker is secure. Make sure the broker and the tunnel server can trust each other. If you disappear from the Internet without closing your tunnel, someone else might get your old address and receive your mail. Tunnel brokers also cannot work if you are behind a private network that hides your address.
